query:
Could a husband force a paternity test and divorce in 1940s New York?

My question is inspired by the Hitchcock film Strangers on a Train.

Our hero, Guy, is married to a woman who has been cheating on him, hounding him for a divorce for a year, and who is now pregnant with a lover's child. Guy is looking forward to the divorce because he's in love with another woman, and wants to be free to marry her. But when he returns home to meet his wife and divorce lawyer, she reveals she has changed her mind about the divorce, intends to force him to stay in the marriage, and also to carry the child. He asks, "Why me? It's not my baby." She replies, "Yes, but people don't know that, Guy."

This is the predicament the movie sets to give the hero a plausible motive for murder. I'm curious how airtight it is.

My question: if Guy could prove his wife had been unfaithful, and that the child was not his, could he obtain a divorce over her objection?

Proof

I assume a paternity test could settle the matter, but they are a relatively recent invention, and for most of the 20th century, tests could only disqualify a significant fraction of the population (Wikipedia: 1920s: 30%; 1930s: 40%; 1960s: 80%). So, the date matters.

The setting's year is ambiguous, there being no title card or other explicit mention of a date. The story was written in 1950 and filmed in '51, but that doesn't mean the movie is set in 1951. In an early scene, the villain tells Guy that he has flown on a "jet plane" -- this may be a fabrication, but Guy understands the phrase, and jets were invented in ~1939, so we can be certain that tests based on serological testing (40% exclusion rate) existed. Guy is a newly-rich tennis star with a Senator as a wannabe father-in-law, so I think we can assume he'd have access to a test -- if the law cared, and if the law would have allowed him to obtain one over his wife's objections.

Jurisdiction

This is also ambiguous and difficult to pin down. Guy and Miriam live in "Metcalf" (and presumably were married there), which it turns out is fictional; those parts of the film were shot in Danbury, Connecticut. (There are real Metcalfs in Georgia and Massachusetts, but those locations are disqualified by other story facts.) The dialogue suggests that Guy's Metcalf is in or near New York. At the time of the murder, he's on a train from New York to Washington. So: New York state.

Would a man of some means, living and married in New York State in the 1940s, have been legally able to obtain a paternity test over his wife's objections, and subsequently divorce her if the test happened to conclusively prove that the child was someone else's?

steps.step_instruction: Investigate the history and availability of paternity testing methods in the 1940s, including their admissibility in court.
Cross-reference societal norms and legal precedents regarding marital disputes and paternal rights in mid-20th century New York.

query:
How do U.S. state laws requiring something from the past interact with U.S. state laws that legally change the past?

In the U.S., state laws can require that someone present some document or information in order to do something. This can be the current version of the thing, or a past version, or, potentially, even the original version.

State laws can also act retroactively,1 making it so that a state of affairs created by the law has, from a legal perspective, existed ever since some date prior to when the law actually took effect.

What happens when one law requires someone to present a past version of something, but another (or even the same) law has retconned that past version out of existence?

As an example, let us imagine the following situation (and assume that all mentioned laws pass state-constitutional muster):2

  1. The U.S. state of Alephistan, governed by the Sodium Party, passes a law to allow trans Alephistanis to change the sex marker on their birth certificates. This law also specifies that sex-marker changes made under this law will be retroactive to the date and time of the person's birth; legally, therefore, an Alephistani who changes the sex marker on their birth certificate has always been the gender corresponding to the updated marker (i.e., a sex-marker change made under this law legally changes the person's AGAB3).
  2. Across the border, the U.S. state of Betaland, governed by the Chlorine Party, instead decides to make it so that trans Betalanders can never update the sex marker on their birth certificates, and also requires that the sex marker on Betaland state IDs correspond to the holder's AGAB. For the latter purpose, it requires Betalanders to present their original birth certificates, minus any later updates, when getting their first state IDs.
  3. Brenda was born and raised in Alephistan. When she popped out of her parent's vagina, the doctor assigned her as male, but, in her late teens, she realizes that she's actually a girl. She changes the sex marker on her Alephistani birth certificate from M to F, which, due to the retroactive nature of the law, makes it so that, legally, the sex marker on her birth certificate has always been F.
  4. Brenda later moves to Betaland and wants to get a Betaland state ID. Under Betaland law, this requires her to present her original Alephistani birth certificate, exactly as it was issued when she was born, before any later updates - and especially before the retroactive change of her birth certificate's sex marker from M to F. However, under Alephistani law, the retroactive nature of the sex-marker change means that the version with the updated sex marker is the original version, and her birth certificate's sex marker has always been F.
  5. Which sex marker will end up on Brenda's Betaland ID card?
  6. In another nearby U.S. state, Seetania, the legislature, split half-and-half, is somewhat indecisive in its course of action. When their law on birth certificates, state IDs, and sex markers is signed into law by the governor, it contains a clause requiring that the sex marker on Seetanian state IDs correspond to the holder's AGAB, as shown on the holder's original birth certificate prior to any later changes (courtesy of the ruling Chlorines), but also, in the same law, a clause making sex-marker changes on Seetanian birth certificates retroactive to the moment of birth (courtesy of an amendment inserted by the Sodium opposition).
  7. Daniel was born and raised in Seetania. When he popped out of his parent's vagina, the doctor assigned him as female, but, in his late teens, he realizes that he's actually a boy. He changes the sex marker on his Seetanian birth certificate from F to M, which, due to the retroactive nature of the law, makes it so that, legally, the sex marker on his birth certificate has always been M.
  8. In his early twenties, Daniel wants to get his first Seetanian state ID. Under Seetanian law, this requires him to present his original Seetanian birth certificate, exactly as it was issued when he was born, before any later updates - and especially before the retroactive change of his birth certificate's sex marker from F to M. However, the very same law also provides that the retroactive nature of the sex-marker change means that the version with the updated sex marker is the original version, and his birth certificate's sex marker has always been M.
  9. Which sex marker will end up on Daniel's Seetanian ID card?

1: Subject to the requirement that they not impose punishment for anything anyone did prior to the law taking effect, as doing so would run afoul of the U.S. Constitution's prohibition of ex post facto laws.

2: I've chosen this particular situation because this was the context in which I originally thought of this question, and also because it could, quite possibly, actually happen in the near future. Nevertheless, this question is of much-more-general applicability, and should not be regarded as limited to the specific situation described.

3: Assigned gender at birth.

steps.step_instruction: Locate case law or legal precedents addressing conflicts between retroactive legal changes and document authenticity requirements.

query:
Rentcharges under Leasehold and Freehold Reform Bill 2024

The Leasehold and Freehold Reform Bill includes Part 7 on estate rentcharges. (A "rentcharge" is an obligation on a freeholder to pay money to a third party known as the "rent owner". This is nothing at all to do with renting property as a tenant).

The 2024 act amends the Law of Property Act 1925 to create a "regulated" rentcharge, and limits the ways that the rent owner can enforce payment. But the definition of a "regulated" rentcharge is:

For the purposes of sections 120B to 122 a rentcharge is “regulated” if it is of a kind that could not be created in accordance with section 2 of the Rentcharges Act 1977.

That section of the 1977 act stopped new rentcharges being created, with a few exceptions. The main exception is "estate rentcharges" where the money goes to maintain land which benefits the householder who has to pay, such as general landscaped areas around a housing estate.

So do I understand correctly that estate rentcharges are of a kind that could be created under the 1977 act, and hence are not "regulated rentcharges" under the 2024 reform act?

If so then it seems that Part 7 of the 2024 act has very little effect, since all other rentcharges have already been extinguished under Section 3 of the 1977 act, or will be by 2037. Have I got that right?

steps.step_instruction: Locate the full text of the Leasehold and Freehold Reform Bill 2024, focusing on Part 7 and its references to regulated rentcharges.
Review the Rentcharges Act 1977, particularly Section 2, to understand the exceptions for estate rentcharges.
Analyze the Law of Property Act 1925 for its original provisions on rentcharges and compare with the 2024 amendments.
Identify any transitional provisions or timelines for extinguishing rentcharges, including the 2037 deadline.
Cross-reference secondary sources or legal commentaries for interpretations of the 2024 act's impact on estate rentcharges.
